content: 1. Administer 7.5 mg of glucagon intravenously over 1 minute or 1-2 mg intramuscularly as a bolus. Intravenous doses exceeding 1 mg may induce nausea and vomiting and are not recommended. 2. After completing the diagnostic procedure, provide oral carbohydrates to fasting patients if it aligns with the diagnostic protocol used. 3. Glucagon is indicated off-label for overdoses of beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. The loading dose is 50-150 mcg/kg intravenously over 1 minute, followed by an infusion of 3-5 mg/hr or 50-100 mcg/kg/hr intravenously. Titrate the infusion to achieve the desired clinical response. 4. Glucagon is indicated for severe hypoglycemic reactions in diabetic patients treated with insulin. Administer oral glucose or intravenous dextrose to replenish glycogen stores. 5. Glucagon has orphan drug designation for the treatment of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (HH). 6. Co-administration of glucagon with anticholinergic drugs, such as aclidinium, atropine, benztropine, dicyclomine, glycopyrrolate, hyoscyamine, ipratropium, methscopolamine, orphenadrine, propantheline, scopolamine, tiotropium, trihexyphenidyl, tropicamide, or umeclidinium, increases the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions due to additive effects on the inhibition of gastrointestinal motility. Avoid or use alternative drugs. 7. Glucagon increases the effects of atropine and toxicity of aclidinium, benztropine, dicyclomine, glycopyrrolate, hyoscyamine, ipratropium, methscopolamine, orphenadrine, propantheline, scopolamine, tiotropium, trihexyphenidyl, tropicamide, and umeclidinium. Avoid or use alternative drugs. 8. Glucagon decreases the toxicity of beta-blockers such as acebutolol, atenolol, betaxolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol, celiprolol, esmolol, labetalol, metoprolol, nadolol, nebivolol, penbutolol, pindolol, propranolol, sotalol, and timolol by sympathetic (adrenergic) effects, including increased blood pressure and heart rate. Use caution and monitor closely. Co-administration may transiently increase pulse and blood pressure. 9. Indomethacin decreases the effects of glucagon through an unknown mechanism. In patients taking indomethacin, glucagon may lose its ability to raise blood glucose or may even cause hypoglycemia. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Glucagon decreases the effects of insulin (including insulin aspart, insulin aspart protamine/insulin aspart, insulin degludec, insulin degludec/insulin aspart, insulin detemir, insulin glargine, insulin glulisine, inhaled insulin, insulin isophane human/insulin regular human, insulin lispro, insulin lispro protamine/insulin lispro, insulin NPH, and insulin regular human) by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. Endogenous glucagon is a regulatory hormone that increases blood glucose levels, while exogenous glucagon is often used to treat hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes mellitus. 11. Glucagon increases the effects of warfarin when doses exceed 50 mg administered over a 2-day period. Monitor closely.
